newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries shave most gains to end slightly up.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries shave most gains to end slightly up.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended modestly higher in volatile trading as strong afternoon selling erased most of the gains posted after the release of a benign fourth quarter employment cost index, analysts said.

The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended up 6/32 at 94-20/32. Its yield, which traded as low as 6.85 percent early in the session, finished the day at 6.93 percent against the 6.94 percent at Monday's close.

The market staged a sharp rally early in the session as prices quickly responded to a surprising smaller-than-expected 0.8 percent rise in the fourth quarter ECI. Wall Street experts had forecast a 0.9 percent rise.

The data, which measure wages and benefit costs combined, eased some inflation fears and pushed back expectations for an interest rate hike at the Federal Reserve's policy setting committee meeting on February 4 and 5.
"The ECI was a big relief to the bond market," said Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at Nationsbanc Capital Market Inc.
The sentiment forced several speculative investors who were holding short positions to run for cover, which fueled the rally even further and sent the benchmark bond up well over a point.
But that soothing feeling did not last long.

Treasury prices lost ground as no follow-through buying after the ECI -- combined with a string of fresh strong retail sales and consumer sentiment data -- prompted frustated longs to dump their positions.

"A lot of the locals in the futures pit I know have been long from early in the morning and they were forced to get out. It was really a one mass of long liquidation at the end of the day," said a trader at a large U.S. investment bank.
U.S. adjusted retail sales, as measured by the Lynch , Jones & Ryan Redbook Retail Sales Index, rose 0.8 percent in the first three weeks of fiscal January versus December.
January consumer confidence rose to 116.8 against a revised 114.2 in December. The data are compiled by the Conference Board.
On top of that, a rumor, later denied, saying that the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) had misreported the ECI data for the Finance, Insurance and Real Estate items also created some unrest.
The afternoon selling spree, however, had already begun when the rumor, which started in the futures pit, hit the cash bond market by late afternoon.
BLS Deputy Commissioner Bill Barron denied the speculative talk. In an interview with Reuters, the official said that "There are no errors in the (ECI) figure."

Players said pension funds could be lured into buying the new securities. "I think there are real money pension fund managers that would buy it as well as some speculative type accounts," said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed down two basis points at 5.05 percent. The six-month bill rate fell three points to 5.11 percent. The year bill rate was down four points at 5.29 percent.

Pundits said jitters ahead of upcoming supply also weighed on prices. "You start to look at the bigger picture and you say, We do have an auction tomorrow," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc.
The Treasury will sell $7.0 billion of new inflation-indexed 10-year notes on Wednesday.
Analysts said investors were likely to show interest if the note yield moves higher than the 3.5 percent plus the consumer price index mark.
The 10-year notes were quoted at 3.5 percent above the CPI in late when-issued trade on Tuesday.

The two-year note closed up 3/32 at 99-21/32, yielding 6.06 percent. The five-year note traded up 5/32 at 99-11/32 to yield 6.41 percent. The ten-year note closed up 7/32 at 98-31/32, yielding 6.64 percent.
